name: Derivatives
kicker: The slope of a curve at a single point · The instantaneous rate of change
briefing: A derivative tells you how fast something is changing at one exact instant, like the reading on a speedometer rather than your average speed for the whole trip. On a graph, it is the slope of the tangent line that just touches the curve at a point. Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz each invented calculus in the late 1600s, and the derivative of position with respect to time is velocity.
answerHtml: derivatives (or differentiation; prompt on slope or rate of change; do not accept “integral”)

prompt: the slope of the tangent line

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Gottfried Leibniz [“LYBE-nits”] first published his calculus in a 1684 paper whose title promised “a new method for maxima and minima, and also tangents.” Joseph-Louis Lagrange [“luh-GRAHNZH”] later introduced the notation that writes this concept with a prime mark after the name of a function.
tossups.r: Leibniz wrote it as d y over d x. For 10 points, name this calculus concept that gives the slope of the tangent line to a curve at a point.

tossups.p: Isaac Newton called this concept a “fluxion” and wrote it with a dot above a letter in his _Method of Fluxions_, which he wrote in 1671 but which was not published until 1736. Bishop George Berkeley’s book _The Analyst_ mocked the vanishing quantities used to define this concept as “ghosts of departed quantities.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, the instantaneous rate of change of a function, which is the reverse of integration.

tossups.p: The first calculus textbook, published in 1696 by the Marquis de l’Hôpital [“loh-pee-TAHL”], included a rule actually discovered by Johann Bernoulli [“ber-NOO-lee”] that finds a limit of the form 0 over 0 by taking this concept of the top and the bottom. Taking this concept of a function twice tells whether its graph curves up or down.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, written f prime of x, which gives the slope of a curve at a point.

tossups.p: Pierre de Fermat [“fair-MAH”] found the highest and lowest points of curves with a method he called “adequality,” decades before Newton and Leibniz developed calculus. A smooth function’s maximum or minimum inside an interval can occur only where this concept equals zero, so setting it equal to zero solves many optimization problems.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept that measures the instantaneous rate of change of a function.

tossups.p: In 1872, Karl Weierstrass [“VY-er-shtrahss”] surprised mathematicians with a function that is continuous everywhere but has this quantity nowhere. The absolute value function has no value of this quantity at zero, because its graph has a sharp corner there.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity from calculus, which equals the slope of the tangent line to a graph.

tossups.p: Michel Rolle proved in 1691 that if a smooth curve starts and ends at the same height, this quantity must equal zero somewhere in between. The mean value theorem generalizes that result: somewhere in between, this quantity equals the slope of the straight line joining the two endpoints.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, written d y over d x, that gives a function’s instantaneous rate of change.

tossups.p: The fourth, fifth, and sixth versions of this concept for an object’s position are jokingly nicknamed snap, crackle, and pop, and the third is called jerk. This concept of velocity with respect to time gives acceleration.
tossups.r: Velocity is this concept of position with respect to time. For 10 points, name this calculus concept that measures an instantaneous rate of change.

tossups.p: Apart from its constant multiples, the function e to the x is the only function that equals its own value of this concept everywhere. This concept of the natural logarithm of x is 1 over x, and this concept of sine of x is cosine of x.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, developed independently by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz, that gives the slope of a curve.

tossups.p: The power rule says that this concept of x to the n equals n times x to the n minus 1, so for x cubed it is 3 x squared. This concept of any constant is zero, since a flat line has no slope.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, which gives the instantaneous rate of change of a function and the slope of its tangent line.

tossups.p: The chain rule finds this concept for a function inside another function, while the product and quotient rules find it for products and quotients of two functions. This concept of a sum is the sum of this concept for each term.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, written f prime of x, which is the reverse of integration.

tossups.p: Economists call this concept of total cost with respect to the number of items made the “marginal cost.” Related rates problems use this concept to find how fast the top of a ladder slides down a wall as its bottom is pulled away.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept that gives the slope of the tangent line, developed by both Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz.

tossups.p: Newton’s method finds a root of an equation by repeatedly subtracting the function’s value divided by this concept, which amounts to following tangent lines down to the x-axis. A point where this concept changes from positive to negative marks a local maximum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept that gives the slope of a curve at a single point.

tossups.p: Augustin-Louis Cauchy [“koh-SHEE”] helped make calculus rigorous by defining this concept as the limit, as h shrinks to zero, of f of x plus h, minus f of x, all over h. That fraction, before the limit is taken, is called a difference quotient.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, which gives the slope of the tangent line and is the reverse of integration.

tossups.p: At an inflection point, the second version of this concept changes sign, so the graph switches between curving up and curving down. If the second version of this concept is positive where the first version is zero, that point is a local minimum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, the instantaneous rate of change, which gives velocity from position.

tossups.p: A 1712 report by the Royal Society, which Isaac Newton secretly helped write, credited Newton over Gottfried Leibniz for inventing the calculus of this concept. Partial versions of this concept, written with a curly d, are used for functions of several variables.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, the slope of a tangent line, which is the opposite of integration.

clues.t: Gives the slope of the tangent line to a curve at a single point
Measures a function’s instantaneous rate of change; velocity is this of position with respect to time
The opposite of integration; the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links the two
Calculus was developed independently by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz in the late 1600s
Written f′(x), read “f prime of x” (Lagrange’s notation), or dy/dx (Leibniz’s notation)
Power rule: for xⁿ it is n xⁿ⁻¹, so for x³ it is 3x²; for any constant it is 0
The chain rule handles a function inside another function; the product and quotient rules handle products and quotients
For eˣ it is eˣ itself; for ln x it is 1/x; for sin x it is cos x, and for cos x it is −sin x
Acceleration is this of velocity (the second one of position); the third one of position is called jerk
At a smooth function’s maximum or minimum it equals 0, so setting it to 0 solves optimization problems
The second one shows concavity: positive means curving up, and it changes sign at an inflection point
Defined as the limit of the difference quotient [f(x + h) − f(x)] / h as h shrinks to 0
Isaac Newton called it a “fluxion” and wrote it with a dot over a letter
A function that has one at a point is continuous there, but |x| is continuous at 0 and has none there (a sharp corner)
Leibniz first published his calculus in 1684, in a paper on “a new method for maxima and minima, and also tangents”
Newton’s _Method of Fluxions_ was written in 1671 but not published until 1736, after his death
Bishop George Berkeley’s _The Analyst_ (1734) mocked the vanishing quantities behind it as “ghosts of departed quantities”
L’Hôpital’s rule, from the first calculus textbook (1696) but found by Johann Bernoulli, uses these to find limits of the form 0/0
Pierre de Fermat’s “adequality” found maxima, minima, and tangent lines decades before Newton and Leibniz
Karl Weierstrass (1872) described a function that is continuous everywhere but has one nowhere
Rolle’s theorem (Michel Rolle, 1691) and the mean value theorem: somewhere between two endpoints, it equals the slope of the line joining them
The fourth, fifth, and sixth ones of position are jokingly nicknamed snap, crackle, and pop
Economists call the one of total cost the marginal cost; related-rates problems use them, like a ladder sliding down a wall
Newton’s method finds roots by repeatedly subtracting a function’s value divided by this, following tangent lines to the x-axis
Augustin-Louis Cauchy made it rigorous by defining it as a limit of difference quotients
A 1712 Royal Society report, which Newton secretly helped write, credited him over Leibniz for inventing calculus
Partial ones, written with a curly d (∂), handle functions of several variables

trap.title: Slope, not area
trap.body: Derivatives and integrals are opposite operations linked by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and both answer lines share clues about Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz. A derivative measures slope or an instantaneous rate of change, while an integral measures area or accumulation. Saying only “slope” or “rate of change” earns a prompt, and a tossup about one named rule (power, chain, product, L’Hôpital’s) may want that rule instead.
trap.fix: Listen for “slope,” “tangent line,” “rate of change,” “velocity from position,” “f prime,” or “d y over d x”: say “derivative.” “Area under a curve,” “antiderivative,” “accumulation,” or the long S symbol mean integral.
trap.line: Real answer line: derivatives (or differentiation; prompt on slope or rate of change; do not accept “integral”)
